body:
# Monókerōs, spelled the way the sources wrote it
Some restorations are cosmetic. **Monókerōs** is not — the marks in this name are the difference between reading the sources and guessing at them.

The Greek tradition is zoological, not mythological: no hero fights the monokeros, no god rides it. Its power lies precisely in being reported — a creature at the edge of the map, described by those who claim to have seen its horn in the flesh. Ktēsias, physician to the Persian king Artaxerxēs, wrote in his Indika of Indian wild asses "swift as horses, with a single horn on the forehead, white at the base, black in the middle, crimson at the tip. " Their horn shavings, he says, are an antidote to all poisons; their fleetness makes them unhuntable.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Monókerōs
- **ASCII form:** monokeros
- **Meaning:** "'Single-horned' (from μόνος + κέρας)"
- **Domain of influence:** Rarity, Ferocity, Wonder
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Μονόκερως
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 157 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **Μονόκερως**. On the evidence, it means "'Single-horned' (from μόνος + κέρας)".

Strip **Monókerōs** to *monokeros* and 2 pieces of evidence vanish:

- **o → ó** — Stress mark (acute/tone): the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.
- **o → ō** — Macron marks the long vowel: the vowel length the ASCII form cannot show.

A reader who knows the marks hears the name correctly on the first try. A reader who never sees them never gets the chance.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Monókerōs** lives at [/sites/monokeros/](/sites/monokeros/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/monokeros/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/monokeros/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/monokeros/patterns/).

The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can say — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it in Tier-1: mechanically verifiable, information-rich.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Monókerōs** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Startups & Venture Creation** — The unicorn: venture capital’s own word for the billion-dollar rarity.
- **Gems, Jewelry & Luxury Materials** — The alicorn outpriced gold; rarity as luxury’s core value.
- **Healthcare, Pharma & Medicine** — The alicorn was antiquity’s antidote; purity-testing is his oldest lore.

The mapping is conservative on purpose: only resonances that can be argued aloud. The rest of the atlas follows the same rule, industry by industry.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Greek tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Theogony](/texts/theogony/), [Homeric Hymns](/texts/homeric-hymns/), and [Works and Days](/texts/works-and-days/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
